text:
We finally moved our billing service off Postgres 11 last weekend — and it was not the clean cutover I promised in the planning doc.

Quick context for people who don't know our stack: the billing DB is about 1.8 TB, most of it in a single invoices_line_items table that nobody has dared to partition since 2019. We used logical replication into a fresh Postgres 16 cluster, let it catch up for nine days, then planned a 20-minute write freeze on Saturday at 06:00 UTC.

What went wrong — in order:

1. Sequences don't replicate with logical replication. We knew this. We had a script for it. The script read sequence values from the wrong schema because someone (me) had hardcoded "public" — and two of our sequences live in "billing_v2". First inserts after cutover hit duplicate key errors for about four minutes.

2. One extension — pg_partman — was on a different minor version on the new cluster. Harmless on its own, but our maintenance job called a function whose signature changed. It failed silently — the job logs to a file nobody reads — and we only noticed Monday when Sunday's partition hadn't been created.

3. The planner chose a terrible plan for our monthly revenue report on 16. Same query, same indexes — 4 seconds on 11, 11 minutes on 16. Running ANALYZE on the big table fixed it. Obvious in hindsight — logical replication doesn't carry statistics — but at 07:30 on a Saturday nothing is obvious.

What went right: the rollback plan was never needed, but having it written down meant nobody panicked. Read replicas switched over with a DNS change and a 60s TTL we had lowered the week before. Customer-facing downtime was 23 minutes against a 20-minute budget.

If you're doing the same upgrade: copy sequences per schema, diff your extension versions with \dx on both sides, and ANALYZE everything before you open the gates. Our runbook is on the engineering blog if anyone wants to steal it — the sequence script is fixed now, I promise.

text:
Three years into running a fully remote team of 14, here's what I actually believe — not what I believed when we started.

Async-first is great for deep work and terrible for onboarding. Our first two remote hires took almost five months to feel productive. We fixed it — partially — by pairing every new hire with a "buddy" for 90 minutes a day during the first three weeks. Retention in year one went from 2 of 4 to 6 of 6.

The weekly all-hands is overrated. We killed ours in March and replaced it with a written Friday update that takes me about 40 minutes to write. Nobody missed the meeting — two people asked for it back after a reorg, and we brought it back for exactly one month.

Timezones matter more than people admit. Having one engineer in Auckland and everyone else between Lisbon and Warsaw meant he was effectively on a different team — not because anyone excluded him, but because every decision happened while he slept. We ended up shifting his role toward on-call and release management, which he actually prefers.

I'm not anti-office — I'd love a place to meet four times a year — but the "remote doesn't work" crowd is mostly describing companies that never changed how they made decisions.

text:
What you're seeing is almost certainly the container being OOM-killed, not your app crashing — exit code 137 is the giveaway. The JVM doesn't know about your cgroup limit the way you think it does, at least not with the flags you posted.

A few things to check, roughly in order:

First — you set -Xmx2g with a container limit of 2Gi. That's the classic mistake. Heap is only part of the JVM's memory. You also have metaspace, thread stacks (1 MB each by default — and Spring Boot with Tomcat will happily spin up 200 threads), the code cache, direct buffers from Netty, and GC overhead. In practice the RSS ends up somewhere around heap + 300–600 MB for a typical Spring service. So the kernel kills you the moment heap fills up even partially past ~1.5 GB.

Second — drop -Xmx entirely and use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 instead. On JDK 17 the JVM reads the cgroup v2 limit correctly, so it'll size the heap relative to the container. 70% is conservative; some people go to 75. I wouldn't go higher unless you've measured.

Third — turn on Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) in a staging pod and run jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary after it's been under load for a while. That tells you exactly where the non-heap memory is going. In our case it was direct buffers — a misconfigured WebClient was allocating a new connection pool per request.

Fourth — check whether the kills line up with your nightly batch job. If kubectl describe pod shows "OOMKilled" and the timestamps cluster around 02:00, that's your answer — the batch loads the whole customer table into memory.

Also — and this is a minor thing — your liveness probe has a 1s timeout. During a full GC pause on a 2 GB heap that can easily fail, and then Kubernetes restarts the pod, which looks a lot like a crash in the logs. Bump it to 5s and set failureThreshold to 3.

If none of that helps, post the output of NMT and I'll take another look.
